title: Application Security & OWASP in Go — Revision

sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Security questions appear in every senior Go engineer interview, and they separate engineers who 'know about security' from those who 'build secure systems by default.' Go's standard library provides strong crypto primitives (crypto/tls, crypto/rand, database/sql parameterised queries), but misuse is easy. Interviewers want to see that you know the OWASP Top 10 in the context of Go services and can point to specific library choices and code patterns that prevent each class of vulnerability.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Layer security at every tier: (1) Input validation at the HTTP boundary. (2) Parameterised queries at the data layer. (3) Short-lived JWTs with RS256 or EdDSA at the auth layer. (4) TLS with mutual authentication at the transport layer. (5) Secrets injected at runtime via vault or environment—never in source. Go's type system helps: use dedicated types (e.g., type UserID int64) to avoid mixing untrusted strings into SQL contexts.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. OWASP Top 10: injection, broken auth, sensitive data exposure, XXE, broken access control, security misconfiguration, XSS, insecure deserialization, vulnerable components, logging failures—and the Go-specific mitigation for each. 2. SQL injection: always use database/sql placeholders ($1, ?), never fmt.Sprintf into queries. 3. JWT: parse with golang-jwt/jwt, validate alg header, verify exp, use RS256 or EdDSA over HS256 in multi-service contexts. 4. OAuth2: golang.org/x/oauth2 for client flows, PKCE for SPAs. 5. TLS: crypto/tls MinVersion TLS 1.2+, certificate pinning, mutual TLS for service-to-service. 6. Secrets management: Vault SDK, AWS Secrets Manager, never os.Getenv for production secrets without rotation. 7. Input validation: go-playground/validator struct tags, explicit allow-lists over block-lists.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: • 'How do you prevent SQL injection in a Go service?' → database/sql parameterised queries, ORM (GORM/sqlc) generated queries, no raw string interpolation. • 'Walk me through how you'd validate and verify a JWT in Go.' → parse header to check alg, verify signature with public key, check exp/nbf/iss claims. • 'How do you store secrets in a Go service on Kubernetes?' → Vault agent injector or AWS Secrets Manager, mount as env vars or files, rotate with SIGHUP handler. • 'What TLS configuration would you use for an internal gRPC service?' → mTLS with client certificates, TLS 1.3, rotate certs via cert-manager.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "My baseline for a secure Go service starts with the transport: I configure crypto/tls with MinVersion set to TLS 1.2 and a restricted cipher suite list. At the auth layer I use JWTs signed with RS256 so each service can verify tokens independently with only a public key—no shared secret. I validate every JWT with golang-jwt/jwt, always checking the alg header to prevent algorithm confusion attacks. For database access I use database/sql with $1 placeholders exclusively—never string interpolation. Secrets come from Vault via the Go SDK; I reload them on SIGHUP without restarting the process. Input validation happens at the handler boundary with go-playground/validator struct tags, and I return a 400 with a sanitised error—never leaking internal details."
